# FREM (Full Random Effects Model)

FREM (Karlsson 2012) is a covariate analysis method that treats covariates as
additional dependent variables, estimating covariate-parameter relationships
through an extended omega matrix rather than explicit covariate models.

## Specifying covariates

The covariates folded into the FREM model — and whether each is **continuous**
or **categorical** — are taken from the model's
[`[covariates]`](../model-file/covariates.qmd) block. That block is the single
source of truth and is **required**: the transformation uses every covariate it
declares.

```text
[covariates]
  WT  continuous
  AGE continuous
  SEX categorical
```

If you don't want *every* declared covariate in the FREM model, pass a
**subset filter** (the `covariates` argument): only the named covariates are
included, and each must be declared in the block. The filter never introduces
covariates the model hasn't declared, nor changes their kind.

## How it works

1. **Data augmentation**: For each subject, pseudo-observation rows are added
   with `DV` set to the subject's covariate value and a `FREMTYPE` column
   distinguishing covariate rows from PK observations.

2. **Model extension**: The base omega is expanded to a full block covering
   both PK random effects and covariate random effects. Covariate thetas are
   fixed at the population mean, and a small covariate sigma (`EPSCOV`) is
   added.

3. **Estimation**: The model is fit normally (FOCEI or SAEM). The off-diagonal
   blocks of the extended omega capture PK-covariate correlations.

## Usage (Rust API)

```rust
use ferx_core::prepare_frem;

let result = prepare_frem(
    &base_model_path,
    &data_path,
    &[],   // empty filter → use every covariate from the model's [covariates] block
    None,  // categorical override (None → kinds come from the [covariates] block)
    None,  // default output model path
    None,  // default output data path
    None,  // missing value indicator (default: -99)
    None,  // no prior fit: keep the base model's declared inits
)?;

// Pass e.g. &["WT".into()] instead of &[] to FREM only a subset of the
// declared covariates.

// result.model_path  — generated FREM .ferx file
// result.data_path   — augmented CSV with FREMTYPE column
// result.n_total_etas — base etas + covariate etas
```

## Usage (R)

```r
library(ferx)

# Covariates (and their continuous/categorical kind) come from the model's
# [covariates] block; omit `covariates` to use all of them.
frem <- ferx_model_to_frem(
  model      = "warfarin.ferx",
  data       = "warfarin_cov.csv",
  output_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "frem")  # default: next to the model file
)
# `output_dir` needs ferx-r from `main` (after 0.3.0). Release 0.3.0 creates the
# directory and then writes next to the model anyway, unless `output_model` and
# `output_data` are both given.

# Or filter to a subset of the declared covariates:
# frem <- ferx_model_to_frem("warfarin.ferx", "warfarin_cov.csv",
#                            covariates = "WT",
#                            output_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "frem"))

fit <- ferx_fit(frem, method = "saem")   # frem is a ferx_model
```

## Interpreting results

- **Covariate omega diagonals** should approximate the sample variance of each
  covariate (since the covariate thetas are fixed at the sample mean).
- **Off-diagonal elements** (or correlations) between PK etas and covariate
  etas reveal covariate-parameter associations.
- A positive correlation between ETA_CL and ETA_WT, for example, indicates
  that subjects with higher weight tend to have higher clearance.

## Estimation method choice

- **SAEM** is recommended for FREM models with many covariates, as the large
  block omega can cause convergence difficulties with gradient-based methods.
- **IMPMAP** with `impmap_mceta` is a strong alternative to SAEM for FREM.
  The multi-start MAP (`impmap_mceta = 3`) helps the per-subject mode search
  escape local optima in the high-dimensional random-effect space. On larger
  FREM models (many covariates / ETAs) where the MAP surface has multiple
  modes, MCETA can dramatically improve importance-sampling efficiency and OFV.
- **FOCEI** works well for smaller FREM models (2-3 covariates) but can
  struggle with large block omegas.

### Warfarin FREM comparison (5 ETAs: 3 PK + WT + AGE, 10 subjects)

All methods use default tuning (SAEM: 500+800 iters; IMPMAP: 200 iters,
K=300). Covariate omega diagonals should approximate sample variances
(WT: 111.6, AGE: 99.4). OFV is the FOCE-Laplace objective.

| Parameter | FOCEI | SAEM | IMPMAP | IMPMAP+MCETA3 |
|-----------|------:|-----:|-------:|--------------:|
| OFV | -177.3 | -220.7 | -220.3 | -220.7 |
| TVCL | 0.133 | 0.133 | 0.133 | 0.133 |
| TVV | 7.73 | 7.74 | 7.74 | 7.74 |
| TVKA | 0.791 | 0.811 | 0.811 | 0.811 |
| ω²(CL) | 0.026 | 0.029 | 0.029 | 0.029 |
| ω²(V) | 0.012 | 0.010 | 0.010 | 0.010 |
| ω²(KA) | 0.351 | 0.336 | 0.336 | 0.336 |
| ω²(WT) | 135.1 | 106.8 | 106.8 | 106.8 |
| ω²(AGE) | 95.1 | 93.8 | 93.8 | 93.8 |
| σ (PROP) | 0.0106 | 0.0105 | 0.0111 | 0.0106 |

FOCEI is ~43 OFV units worse and overestimates the covariate variances,
while SAEM, IMPMAP, and IMPMAP+MCETA3 all agree closely. On this small model
(5 ETAs) the MCETA benefit is modest (~0.4 OFV); on larger FREM models with
many covariates the improvement can be dramatic.

::: {.callout-note}
## The FOCEI column has moved since this table was measured

Two fixes landed on the FOCEI arm of this fixture. Its Nelder–Mead inner-loop
restart used to reset a FREM covariate eta to zero, tens of units from where its
pseudo-observation pins it, and the reported OFV used to be read off a **cold** EBE
re-solve rather than the one the optimizer minimised
([#1349](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1349),
[#833](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/833)). Re-measured 2026-09-13
on the fix, the Linux arm reaches **OFV −220.7** — the same value SAEM and IMPMAP
reach above — while the macOS arm lands at **−174.9** in a different basin, with
ω²(V) and ω²(KA) inflated. That remaining platform split is
[#990](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/990); the FOCEI row above
predates both fixes and is kept as the historical measurement rather than
half-updated.
:::

## IIV on residual error (`iiv_on_ruv`) {#frem-iiv-on-ruv}

### The residual-error eta stays out of the covariate block

An `iiv_on_ruv` eta scales the residual SD. It is not a structural parameter, so
covariates do not explain it. `prepare_frem()` therefore emits it as its own diagonal
`omega` outside the FREM `block_omega`. It keeps a `FIX` and a prior fit's value.
This is the structure NONMEM / PsN FREM use (a separate `$OMEGA` for the IIV-on-RUV
eta). Before [#904](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/904) the generator
put it inside the block, with a nonzero starting covariance to every covariate eta. If
the base model correlates it with a PK eta (`block_omega (ETA_CL, ETA_RUV)`), it stays
in the block so that covariance is kept, but it starts with no covariate cross-terms.

On the 475-subject, 8-covariate workshop reprex of #904, the old layout is a superset
model. It has 11 extra covariances, which estimate to small values (|ρ| ≤ 0.22). Under
SAEM it scores 6851.2 ± 0.8 importance-sampled −2 log L, against 6866.6 ± 1.2 for the
split layout. A 15-unit drop for 11 parameters is not significant (χ²₁₁, p ≈ 0.17).
The change is a structural match to NONMEM, not a fix for the σ × ω_RUV runaway; that
fix is [η_RUV re-centring](saem.qmd#iiv-on-residual-error-iiv_on_ruv-σ-ω_ruv-ridge).

### Which estimator

Measured on the #904 reprex (split layout, σ started 5.5× low at 0.032), Linux,
2026-10-16. In the two FOCEI rows the zero covariate–covariate covariances are
1e-4 in both engines, because NONMEM refuses a zero inside a non-band `BLOCK`.

| Estimator | ω_RUV | σ | objective |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| ferx SAEM (`n_exploration = n_convergence = 1000`, `n_mh_steps = 50`) | 0.269 | 0.174 | IS −2 log L 6866.6 ± 1.2 (K = 20000) |
| NONMEM 7.6 IMP `EONLY=1` at the ferx SAEM estimates (`ISAMPLE=20000`) | 0.269 | 0.174 | 6869.7 (mean of iterations 2–6, sd 1.2) |
| NONMEM IMP, as reported in #904 (`run6_imp`) | 0.279 | 0.177 | 6852 |
| ferx FOCEI | 0.298 | 0.032 | 12039.4523, never leaves the start |
| NONMEM 7.6 FOCEI, same start | 0.298 | 0.032 | 12039.4523, `MINIMIZATION TERMINATED` at the start |

Scored at the same point, the two engines' importance-sampled objectives agree to
about 3 units. ferx integrates the FREM covariate etas out analytically
(`frem_rao_blackwell`) and NONMEM samples them, so the two estimators are not
identical.

Use **SAEM** (or IMPMAP), and compare fits by the importance-sampled objective
(`imp_eval_only = true`, `imp_samples = 20000`). The FOCE objective is not a
reliable ranking tool for `iiv_on_ruv` (see [SAEM](saem.qmd#the-focei-objective-cannot-rank-iiv_on_ruv-fits)).
**FOCEI** fails on this model in NONMEM too: both engines report the same objective
at the start to every printed digit, and neither moves from it. On the same data
without the covariate rows, FOCEI estimates ω_RUV = 0.058 in ferx and 0.062 in
NONMEM, against ≈ 0.28 from SAEM / IMP. At the start the two objectives agree to
every printed digit (549.7913), and ferx's optimum is 23 units lower than NONMEM's.
Both engines underestimate ω_RUV, so that is a property of the FOCE approximation,
not of ferx. Standalone `method = imp` on large
FREM models is tracked in [#1365](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1365).

## Limitations

- Categorical covariates are binarized (one-hot encoded) before the FREM
  transformation.
- FREM is defined for Gaussian endpoints only. A model with a non-Gaussian
  endpoint (`[event_model]`, `[binary_model]`, a Markov block) is refused by
  `prepare_frem()` / `transform_dataset_for_frem()` with
  `E_FREM_NON_GAUSSIAN_ENDPOINT`: the transformed dataset is written from the
  Gaussian rows only, so the endpoint's rows would be lost. Run the FREM step on
  the PK model without that block
  ([#1199](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1199)).
- The `prepare_frem()` API handles the full transformation; manual FREM model
  construction is not recommended.
